newsitem.title: TURKEY: Incoming Turkish government inherits tough job.
newsitem.headline: Incoming Turkish government inherits tough job.

text.p: Turkey's new secularist prime minister Mesut Yilmaz faces a parliamentary debate on his plan of action on Thursday knowing that his government will find it hard to keep all its promises.
Yilmaz looks set to win the vote of confidence scheduled for July 12 but with early polls looming, his new coalition faces challenges at home and abroad.
A government programme read out in parliament this week gave no date for polls, but a key left-wing party backing the alliance has made clear its support is linked to early elections.
Analysts say Yilmaz, a conservative, can hold out for at most a year before his ally withdraws support.

His Motherland Party has been joined by another leftist party and a right-wing grouping and on paper the alliance is a good dozen MPs clear of the majority needed to win the confidence of the 550-member assembly.
But then the job will really begin.
The incoming economy and finance ministers on Wednesday described the gloomy economic position they had inherited from the previous Islamist-led government.

Finance Minister Zekeriya Temizel told a news conference that figures for the first half of the year showed a deficit of 720 trillion lira ($4.8 billion), despite Islamist former prime minister Necmettin Erbakan's promises of a balanced 1997 budget.
Gunes Taner, leader of the incoming economics team, promised no grand reforms. "Our aim is not to take shock decisions...but to sort out this business with fine tuning," he said.
The government programme has promised to speed up work to privatise state-owned banks.
In foreign policy, the government has pledged to push for NATO-member Turkey's full membership of the European Union.
But a feverish economy, rows with neighbouring EU-member Greece and a poor human rights record make full membership look like an ambitious aim.
Additionally, the secular military expects the government to take long-delayed and controversial measures to rein in growing religious radicalism, especially in the education system.
The government pledges to put before parliament a plan to extend compulsory education to eight years from five, at the expense of religious schools.
But the coalition can expect fierce opposition from the ousted Islamists -- still the biggest party in parliament -- to the education reforms demanded by the military in February.
It was military pressure, combined with help from the president and the near collapse of a rival party, that gave Yilmaz the chance to become prime minister.

Yilmaz's Islamist predecessor Necmettin Erbakan stepped down last month in a bungled plan to have his junior partner Tansu Ciller take over power. The Islamist-led coalition had been buckling under pressure from the secularist military.
But Demirel bypassed Ciller and handed the mandate straight to Yilmaz, even though the secular conservative was short of a parliamentary majority.
That lack of backing from MPs, however, was soon bridged by a flood of defections from Ciller's party to its rival, Yilmaz's Motherland.
($1 = 150,900 Turkish lira)
